subject: physiology
title: Nerve Fibre Vulnerability, Degeneration, and Regeneration

steps.tx: Different nerve fibre types display distinct susceptibilities to physiological insults. When subjected to ischaemia, **susceptibility to hypoxia** is greatest in large myelinated A fibres, intermediate in B fibres, and lowest in unmyelinated C fibres. Because large A fibres possess high metabolic energy demands for continuous sodium pumping, tourniquet ischaemia paralyses motor and touch senses while sparing dull pain.
steps.say: Large myelinated A fibres are most vulnerable to hypoxia because of high metabolic demands, while unmyelinated C fibres are most resistant.

steps.tx: Mechanical compression blocks nerve conduction by displacing myelin and producing localized microvascular ischaemia. Heavy mechanical pressure preferentially impairs large myelinated **A-alpha fibres**, causing motor weakness and loss of proprioception and vibration sense. This vulnerability explains wrist drop in Saturday night radial nerve palsy and tourniquet paralysis, while dull unmyelinated C fibre pain remains intact.
steps.say: Mechanical compression preferentially damages large A fibres, causing motor paralysis and numbness while leaving unmyelinated pain fibres functioning.

left.title: Pressure Palsy (Saturday Night Radial)
points: Direct mechanical compression of large A fibres
C fibre burning pain remains unaffected

right.title: Local Anaesthetic Block
points: Chemical blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels
Small diameter A-delta and C fibres blocked first
Loss of pain and temperature precedes motor block
Large motor A-alpha fibres blocked last

steps.tx: In contrast to hypoxia and pressure, pharmacological **local anaesthetics** exhibit an inverse sequence of susceptibility. Small unmyelinated C fibres and thinly myelinated A-delta fibres are blocked first, followed by small B fibres, with large motor A-alpha fibres blocked last. Shorter critical lengths of exposure and high firing rates render small pain fibres exceptionally vulnerable to sodium channel blockade.
steps.say: Local anaesthetics block small unmyelinated C and A-delta fibres first, abolishing pain and temperature before affecting large motor fibres.

steps.tx: Complete axonal transection initiates an anterograde degenerative cascade distal to the injury site termed **Wallerian degeneration**. Deprived of vital somal axoplasmic transport, the distal axon segment swells, fragments, and is cleared by recruited macrophages. Surrounding Schwann cells dedifferentiate, shed their myelin sheaths, and proliferate along the original endoneurial basal lamina.
steps.say: Wallerian degeneration destroys the axon distal to a transection. Macrophages clear debris while Schwann cells proliferate inside endoneurial tubes.

nodes.label: Axonal Transection (Axotomy) Separates Distal Segment from Soma
Axon Fragments & Macrophages Clear Axoplasm and Myelin Debris
Schwann Cells Proliferate to Form Bands of Bungner
Proximal Growth Cone Sprouts and Navigates Toward Target

steps.tx: The proliferating Schwann cells form column-like cellular conduits designated bands of Bungner within intact endoneurial tubes. In peripheral nerves, **nerve regeneration** proceeds at a steady rate of one to two millimetres per day (approximately one inch per month) as axonal growth cones sprout from the proximal stump, guided by neurotropic factors toward terminal target end-organs.
steps.say: Peripheral nerve axons regenerate at one to two millimetres per day along Schwann cell bands of Bungner toward their target organs.

steps.tx: Simultaneously, the cell body undergoes reactive retrograde alterations designated **chromatolysis**. Within forty-eight hours of axotomy, the neuronal nucleus shifts eccentric to the periphery, the perikaryon swells, and Nissl granules disperse as the cell transitions from neurotransmitter production to high-volume structural protein and RNA synthesis required for axonal repair.
steps.say: Chromatolysis occurs in the cell body after axotomy. The nucleus moves peripherally and Nissl substance disperses as protein synthesis accelerates for repair.

left.title: Normal Resting Neuron
points: Centrally placed round nucleus with prominent nucleolus
Abundant coarse Nissl substance (rough ER clusters)
Stable synaptic architecture with dendritic spines

right.title: Chromatolytic Axotomized Neuron
points: Eccentrically displaced nucleus at cell periphery
Dispersal of Nissl granules into fine cytoplasmic dust
Dramatically upregulated tubulin and actin synthesis

steps.tx: Survival and guided directional outgrowth of regenerating axons depend strictly on target-derived polypeptides called **neurotrophins**. The prototype nerve growth factor (NGF), along with brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), neurotrophin-3, and neurotrophin-4/5, bind high-affinity Trk receptor tyrosine kinases, undergoing retrograde axonal transport to the soma to suppress apoptotic caspase activation.
steps.say: Target-derived neurotrophins such as nerve growth factor bind Trk receptors and undergo retrograde transport to promote neuronal survival and guide outgrowth.

Binding and Dimerization of High-Affinity Trk Tyrosine Kinase Receptors

steps.tx: The adult central nervous system posts molecular no entry signs against regrowth. **Nogo-A**, a myelin protein, collapses growth cones that touch it, helping explain why spinal cord axons regenerate so poorly while peripheral nerves succeed. Blocking it and its partners is an active research route to cord repair. The contrast between peripheral success and central failure is one of neurology most practical examination themes.
steps.say: Myelin Nogo-A blocks central axon regrowth, unlike the permissive peripheral nerve. Blocking it is a research route to spinal repair.

vis.alt: Image showing Nogo-A in central myelin inhibiting axon growth cone advance.
vis.caption: A growth cone is shown halted at myelin bearing the Nogo-A signal. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: In contrast to peripheral nerves, central axonal regeneration fails because oligodendrocytes express potent inhibitory surface ligands such as **Nogo-A**, myelin-associated glycoprotein, and oligodendrocyte myelin glycoprotein. Furthermore, reactive astrocytes proliferate to establish a dense impenetrable physical and chemical glial scar containing chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, halting axonal growth cone elongation in the spinal cord.
steps.say: Central regeneration fails because oligodendrocytes express inhibitory Nogo-A while astrocytes form an impenetrable glial scar that blocks growth cones.
